title: Sailors missing after fresh attacks on Black Sea vessels, Bulgaria says
content: One merchant ship has sunk and its crew is missing after a drone attack in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say. A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its crew of 18 were rescued. Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine. Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said. The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. It was not clear how many crew members were on board. A search operation has been launched. The vessel's cargo was not immediately known. Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. The vessel was carrying grain. Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law". He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable." Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea. A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media. On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks. Arkadii Petrov - who attended Kirkcudbright Academy - is honoured at the Ukrainian Chapel in Lockerbie. The vessel's captain was killed and 11 crew members were rescued after the attack on the Turkish-owned ship, Ukraine's leader says. title: Nigeria mourns 32 killed as military plane crashes into swamp
content: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 32 people. Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down in a swamp near a naval base on Monday morning. After reaching the site, the aircraft was found to be submerged under water, officials said. A resident told the BBC that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area. It is the deadliest crash involving a Nigerian military aircraft since 1992. Tinubu offered his deepest condolences for the 25 passengers and seven crew members on board and has ordered a full investigation. The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died. "This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said. "Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added. Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today". He said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state. He said search and rescue efforts were ongoing. The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers. The Nigerian Air Force has released the names of those killed, showing that most of those on board were military personnel. Tinubu has ordered the Air Force to immediately begin a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to help prevent similar incidents in the future. The Nigerian Air Force plays a key role in the country's military operations, including efforts to tackle armed groups and insecurity in several parts of the country. In May 2021, Nigeria's army chief, Lt-Gen Ibrahim Attahiru, was killed in a plane crash alongside 10 other officers in the north-western state of Kaduna amid bad weather. title: Trump says he will stop using taxpayer funds for ads after bipartisan pushback
content: President Donald Trump has said he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television ads he has fronted, following bipartisan pushback. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," he said Monday on social media. Trump said it is "a rather standard thing to do" but that he has decided to pay for the "Patriotic Ads" himself and with money he raised through his MAGA Inc super political action committee. The ads, which praise the president and his policies, drew criticism and questions over their legality due to laws against using government money for political ads. There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the "deep state" and others he perceives as enemies. In one ad, Trump says, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all". The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections , when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump's approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing - and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress. The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads "educational" and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements. They've pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines. But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies. "It's difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president," legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC. Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads. "It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language 'paid for by the U.S. Government,' should not be paid for by the United States government," the measure reads. The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle. Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while "I like the message ... it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars". Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads. "I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," the Louisiana lawmaker said. title: Tories pledge £10bn British 'Iron Dome' air defence system
content: The Conservatives have pledged to invest £10bn in a British defence system, if they win the next general election, which is inspired by Israel's Iron Dome air defence system. The party said the "Britannia Shield" would offer the UK an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said it would help protect the country against a "new type of warfare" that could see drones and missiles attacking critical national infrastructure. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Tories had an "abysmal record" of defending Britain during their 14 years in power, adding: "They owe Britain an apology, not another lecture." The party said the air defence system would be capable of defending the UK's critical national infrastructure, military bases and sovereign territories from sophisticated threats. Badenoch said that the £10bn would be split over 10 years, with £1bn allocated each year for the project. Earlier this year, Gen Sir Richard Barrens told MPs on the Commons Defence Select Committee "the cost of an iron dome at entry level is probably £80bn over 10 years". Although the Conservatives said the system would be "in essence a British 'Iron Dome'", Badenoch appeared to draw back from that comparison in broadcast interviews. Speaking to the BBC, she said: "We are not building the Iron Dome... We are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here." She said the system would not be "exactly what Israel has" and that the UK needs to start "thinking ahead" to ensure it can protect itself against hostile missiles and drones. She said she had been listening to figures like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and following the impact of the war in Iran on Gulf countries when crafting her plans. "Warfare is changing," she said. "It isn't just missiles coming from very far afield anymore, what we are seeing with drone technology is that people can get close enough to fire drones at the UK." The Tories added the proposal would strengthen the UK's air defence systems at a time when Nato allies have warned they are facing repeated Russian drone incursions. The party also cited a report from the defence committee of MPs last November which said the UK was lagging behind its European counterparts in having a plan to defend itself and overseas territories from a military attack. The Conservatives said the system would have three components - new advanced radar systems, upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain's defences and rapidly decide a response, and new interceptor missiles as well as counter-drone capabilities. The three-tiered design of the proposal is similar to the British Army's current Sky Sabre air defence system. This system - which can intercept munitions and aircraft as well as integrate with wider air defences - was deployed by the UK to the Middle East earlier this year for defensive action against Iranian attacks. Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the defence and security think thank RUSI (the Royal United Services Institute), said £10bn would "probably cover" what the UK "actually needs" including horizon radar and more E7 aircrafts. "In contrast, if what the Conservatives envision is a truly Israeli style multi-layered missile defence system, £10bn probably wouldn't get there," he said. "But that system would also be quite superfluous, arguably." Prof Steven Barrett, CEO of Cambridge Aerospace which has been developing interceptor missiles, told the BBC £10bn was a "significant commitment" but the exact cost of the project would depend on the detail of the Conservatives' proposal. He said that it would not be practical for the system to defend "every square inch" of UK territory and a more plausible set up would cover "significant parts of the population in key high density areas". He also said there needed to be a focus on protecting critical national infrastructure, adding that a" huge amount of damage" could be done if data centres used by transport and health systems came under attack. In his speech at the conference in Birmingham, shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge will say: "With a £10bn budget, this would be one of Britain's most significant military programmes since the cold war. "But one that is totally necessary because of the threats we face." Streeting said in response: "They [the Conservatives] cut the Army to its smallest size since Napoleon and left a £17bn hole in the equipment plan. "Their own defence secretary, Ben Wallace, admitted our Armed Forces had been 'hollowed out and underfunded'." The Conservatives said their plan would be funded within their existing commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of existing expenditure. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been under pressure to set out how he will reach Nato's 3.5% of GDP spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year. The current Labour government's Defence Investment Plan includes more than £350m to double the number of Sky Sabre systems operated by the British Army, with ground-based air defence sitting alongside air and maritime capabilities. title: ASOS app users receive push notifications apparently sent by hackers
content: Asos users across the UK have been sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company. Dozens of people have told the BBC about receiving a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app, appearing on their phone screens. "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message reads. Asos did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for comment. "If confirmed, this is a deeply serious attack because the hackers appear to have done something particularly brazen: turned ASOS's own app into their ransom note," says Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point. "Millions of people trust notifications from apps on their phones because they are supposed to come directly from the company." On social media, dozens of people have posted about receiving the message - confused as to what it means. Although the apparent extortion message has been issued directly to customers, it is addressed to Asos' data protection officer (DPO) and IT team. The message claims the unnamed hackers have "fully compromised the Snowflake instance". This refers to the data storage company Snowflake, whose tools are used by dozens of firms for collecting, analysing and storing data. It is not known if ASOS is a customer of Snowflake or what data, if any, is stored with the service. But Snowflake has been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years and has been linked to incidents targeting services including Ticketmaster and Santander . It is, however, very unusual for a data breach to be revealed quite so publicly - and for customers to be informed in this manner. Most extortions and negotiations by cyber criminals are conducted in private, with hackers hoping their discretion will result in a quiet pay-off. The pop up message contains a link to the hackers' Telegram channel. The new group is calling itself Xuanye Group and only created it's Telegram channel today. They have posted only three times with the latest being about the ASOS hack. Dan Bird, from cyber security firm Horizon3 says the pop up message the criminals sent implies that their access has gone beyond the Snowflake database. "Sending a push notification to ASOS's app users would require access to the company's notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised." "If both claims hold up, it suggests the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door," he said. title: Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway
content: Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement. The Yemeni military also said in a statement that its forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes. But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources later told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces had only reached the city's outskirts. The Houthis denied losing Bab al-Mandab and Mokha and said they had struck Riyadh's airport and other locations in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the air strikes. Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks and reiterated calls for the UN Security Council's permanent members to support Yemen's internationally-recognised government. Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, meanwhile held an emergency meeting in Riyadh and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia in an invocation of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, according to a statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP. The offensive launched by the pro-government National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces in south-western Yemen on Monday reportedly saw the Houthis pushed out of most of the coastal areas they seized last month. Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating. Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said: "Our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area." Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town. Houthi‑run media cited a Houthi military source as rejecting as "Saudi propaganda" the claims that the group had lost control of Mokha, and that the group remained in control of Dhubab, Bab al‑Mandab and the Kahboub mountains near the coast. The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital, Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago. Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive. Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV. Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences". The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations". On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis. Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia". It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded. The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory. In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram. According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east. A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island. They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia. However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry. The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced. title: Former American Idol contestant sentenced to life in prison for murdering wife
content: A US man who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for murdering his wife. Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty last week after a short deliberation by the jury, which rejected his claim that an intruder broke into his Ohio home and shot his wife, Ashley Flynn, as she slept. He was also found guilty of eight additional charges, including aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. Letters from his two daughters were read in court during the sentencing hearing on Monday, pleading with him to finally admit his guilt and questioning why he killed their mother. Flynn, a former music pastor, fatally shot his wife, a 37-year-old teacher, in February before staging their home in Tipp City to appear as if someone had broken in through the garage. Flynn claims he was asleep when he heard gunshots and found his wife dead in bed after finding the garage door open. Their two children, ages 9 and 11, were also sleeping in the house at the time. His wife's sister, Kayla Keyt, read a victim impact statement saying the murder had caused his daughters to question their Christian faith and had "shattered a family who trusted you". One of his daughter's letters read: "Dear Daddy, I don't even know where to start. How could you do such a thing?" She also said: "Mommy was the perfect person... And then you chose to kill the only mother I ever had." The other daughter's letter began "Dear Caleb", rather than addressing him as her father, and asked him to "tell everyone what you did it and receive your outcome". "You made me feel like an idiot thinking I could trust you," his daughter said. She added that she continues to have faith in God, and that she will never visit her father in prison. Flynn sobbed loudly as the letters from his children were read. The sentencing hearing also included Flynn reading a statement expressing love for his family, apologising for unspecified "decisions" that he made, and again claiming that he did not kill his wife. "I made vows to Ashley on our wedding day. I failed those vows," he said. Judge Jeannine Pratt called Flynn an "extreme" risk to the public as she imposed her sentence. The murder verdict last week followed eight days of testimony, during which several incriminating text messages Flynn sent to his former mistress, Alleigha Botner, were read out and AI-generated songs were played that prosecutors said he made for her. Evidence presented during trial included police body camera footage and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch from around the time of the murder when he claimed to have been sleeping. The prosecution also called dozens of witnesses, including Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church. Botner read aloud in court some of their 100,000 text messages, including one where Flynn wrote: "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail." In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone." Flynn did not testify during the trial, and his defence team called no witnesses. His lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, has said he plans to file a notice of appeal, telling reporters last week: "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design." Mulligan argued that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder and questioned why Flynn was being accused of tampering with evidence because his gun could not be found. This gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open. Prosecutor Paul Watkins read a statement from Ashley Flynn's family in court after the verdict in September, saying: "Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart." "She loved people," the statement continued. "Most of all, she loved being a Mum." Flynn briefly appeared on American Idol in 2013, saying that he loved his wife "more than anything". title: Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
content: Bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86. Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset. In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions. The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star. Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset, where his family bought a house from John Cleese's mother. In 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth. He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman. He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001. He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages. The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker. The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story. He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial. He was released in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news". "We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday. Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently." Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world." Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered". Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday. Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form. "He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience." Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him." Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer". James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer. Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company." Michael Grade, who produced the TV adaptation of Archer's Kane and Abel, told BBC Breakfast he "was a consummate storyteller in real life as as well as on on the page". "That was his greatest skill. But his greatest regret, I'm sure, was that he wasn't able to fulfil his political ambitions. I think he always secretly wanted to be - not necessarily so secretly - to be prime minister. "But because of the mistakes he made in his life, it wasn't for me. But he loved politics more than anything," Lord Grade said. Kate Elton, CEO of Archer's publisher HarperCollins, told BBC's Radio 4 Today programme: "He was curious about everybody and everything and he was just enormous fun." Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book . "It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School. Archer had been due to attend the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel. He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said. The couple have two sons and five grandchildren. title: Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
content: Officials in California denounced comments made by President Donald Trump as “dangerous” on Monday after he appeared to suggest Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego – major cities in a state he has often criticized. Trump was speaking at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska , ahead of the midterm elections and said he wanted to see “a tremendous victory because it verifies all the things we did.” The president called the war with Iran a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” adding that Iran could take out a city. “Let, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s this is a very small price to pay and it’s gonna be over with very soon,” Trump said in comments that drew swift backlash from California’s leaders. CNN has reached out to the White House for more information on what Trump meant by his comments about the two cities. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom called the president “deranged and dangerous,” while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the statements against the city “could potentially compromise our safety.” “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” said Bass, also a Democrat. The Democratic mayor of San Diego, Todd Gloria, said the city “is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” The president went on to say that the war is “going to end very soon.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Trump may be in political trouble. But Trump-style global populism isn’t
content: President Donald Trump might be in a political hole, but his brand of conservative populist nationalism is flourishing across the globe. Rising star Flávio Bolsonaro’s shock win in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election Sunday bolstered Trump’s project of remaking the Western Hemisphere in his political image. Populist right-wingers are also on the march in Europe, fueled by the same failures of foreign leaders to tackle the cost of living and deliver promised change that are haunting US Republicans as the midterm elections draw near. The radical anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) is catapulting into a national force as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government flatlines. France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. These parties aren’t Trump clones, and some predate his MAGA movement. But his rise to power and endurance inspire them. And the administration loudly supports its nationalist brethren threatening to topple the centrist European leaders the president meets at international summits . Many far-right parties share the populist ethos that powered Trump’s stunning 2016 and 2024 campaigns, embracing protectionist economics and emulating his hostility to elites, globalization and mass immigration. It would be ironic if right-wing populists peak elsewhere just as Trump’s star fades . But he makes an unlikely lame duck, and may copy other second-term presidents who aggressively tried to imprint their legacies on the world before leaving power. The strength of conservative populism has conjured an existential moment for leaders like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and his new British counterpart Andy Burnham . Both are leading a fight-back by adopting rhetoric and programs designed to blunt the right and reinforce moderate, centrist government. But Trump’s violent political shifts seem to be stirring a separate counter-reaction, especially in the United States, as the success of democratic socialists in some midterm primaries heralds a new wave of left-wing populism. Bolsonaro is the eldest son of Trump buddy and former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro , who was imprisoned after being convicted of plotting a coup against Brazil’s current leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva after 2022 general elections. Lula has only three weeks before a runoff election to mount a comeback that would stop the most populous Latin American democracy from careening to the right. Trump will loom large over the second round after Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Tim Kaine and Peter Welch wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month to accuse the administration of using tariffs and economic sanctions to interfere in Brazilian democracy. Trump, meanwhile, marked Brazil’s Sunday election by casting doubt on America’s democracy, noting that 125 million people voted and results came out the same day, unlike in some US states. “Voting in America is CORRUPT !!!” he posted . Bolsonaro Jr.’s surprising ascent follows that of Abelardo De La Espriella , a right-wing insurgent who won Colombia’s presidential election earlier this year. Conservative governments friendly to the White House now rule in Costa Rica, after the election of populist Laura Fernández Delgado, and in El Salvador, Chile and Honduras. In Argentina, President Javier Milei, the Trump acolyte who gifted a chainsaw to Elon Musk at a conservative conference, benefited from a $20 billion currency swap offer Trump made conditional on voters supporting his party in legislative elections. Trump is also stamping his influence on the region by propping up the leftist authoritarian Venezuelan regime while concluding oil-exporting deals that critics have styled as 21st-century imperialist plunder. The populist tide may lift one of the right-wing nationalist movement’s most abiding figures in France next year after three previous failed presidential bids. Le Pen has in the past been thwarted by her country’s two-stage electoral system as voters coalesced around moderate rivals. But the collapse of establishment center-right and center-left parties means she may face left-wing populist Jean-Luc Mélenchon — whom she’s currently expected to beat — in a runoff. Le Pen has remodeled her National Rally party, which evolved from the National Front of her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen. But she still advocates nationalist, anti-immigration, protectionist policies and antipathy to the EU. She’d be the most right-wing French president of the modern era and would shake the establishments in Paris and Brussels just as Trump did in Washington. European centrists are even more alarmed by the AfD, since far-right parties court particular notoriety in Germany, which has spent 80 years processing the shame of Nazism. The AfD is to the right of Le Pen and MAGA, and its critics accuse it of historical denialism, antisemitism and ethno-nationalism. But it’s now the second biggest single party in Germany’s federal legislature. In 2025, Vice President JD Vance outraged Europeans by meeting the AfD leader Alice Weidel in Munich while warning that immigration was destroying Western civilization. Last month, Trump backed the AfD on social media after a landslide win in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, writing, “THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore!” Trump has long projected leadership over global populism. He claimed in 2016, for instance, that he “called” Britain’s vote to leave the EU, which was a harbinger of his own populist surge to the presidency a few months later. But he’s not had things all his own way. Far-right MAGA hero and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán fell from power this year despite Trump’s efforts to save him. And the president’s friendship with another conservative populist, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , soured over the Iran war and his claim that she “begged” him for a selfie. Carney reacted to Trump’s demands for Canada to become the 51st state by emerging as an informal leader of the Western democracies in a role vacated by Trump. In January, he warned that at “a time of rising populism and ethnic nationalism, Canada can show how diversity can be a strength, not a weakness.” Burnham used his speech at the Labour Party annual conference last week to address the resentment arising from economic blight that feeds right-wing populism. He blamed the “British Right” dating back to Margaret Thatcher’s governments of the 1980s for pushing deregulation, de-industrialization and privatization. But if Burnham fails, Trump’s populist pal and Reform leader Nigel Farage is waiting to pounce. Burnham sounds a little like former President Joe Biden, who tried to drain the well of Trumpism in decaying post-industrial areas with vast infrastructure and social spending bills. But Biden long underestimated the size of the task. He said back in 2012 that he expected the “fever” of radical conservatism to break and later forecast a GOP “epiphany” after Trump left office in 2020. Trump-style populism may wax and wane, but its resilience suggests it’s now a permanent feature in global democracies, whatever the political fates have in store for its patron.

title: US and China discussing reciprocal nuclear site visits amid concerns about a new arms race
content: The Trump administration has discussed beginning reciprocal nuclear site visits with China and plans to continue pushing for that possibility during in-person meetings in the coming months, according to sources familiar with the matter. The discussions, which have been informal and preliminary, come amid mounting US concerns about China’s rapidly growing nuclear weapons program and after the last remaining arms control agreement between the US and Russia expired last year. The effort to establish a trilateral agreement began in Trump’s first term, but no tangible progress has been made and formal talks on a new accord have not begun, with China and Russia largely ignoring substantive US outreach efforts. The idea of reciprocal visits was initially raised by the Chinese while meeting US officials this year, one source said, giving some indication that the communist nation may be open to pursuing confidence building measures that could pave the way for a grander agreement. Visits to the US Department of Energy national labs and to China’s equivalent facilities were discussed, and the US would be open to discussing visits to nuclear testing sites, the source said. The nuclear discussions between the US and Chinese officials at the working level so far this year have largely occurred on the sidelines of gatherings by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, known as the P5, sources said. The concept of allowing nuclear site visits could move the needle on the US efforts to engage China on issues related to strategic stability and potentially serve as a building block for a trilateral agreement, but China remains adamant that they will not engage on discussions that could limit their nuclear buildup. The US currently has a much bigger nuclear arsenal with about 5,000 total nuclear warheads while China has about 600, but it is expanding its nuclear weapons infrastructure and has been projected to produce hundreds more warheads over the next decade. A State Department spokesperson referred questions to the White House, which did not provide a comment. CNN has requested comment from the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. Last Thursday, China began its weeklong National Day holiday, during which all government offices are closed. Paul Dean, who previously served as an acting assistant secretary of state overseeing US arms control efforts, told CNN that the administration needs to approach any Chinese nuclear negotiations with its “eyes wide open,” but said that reciprocal visits would be “an extremely valuable confidence-building measure” that could lay the informational and diplomatic foundation for additional work to reduce nuclear risk between the two countries. “This is a very dangerous time, and there are very few guardrails in place on the US-China nuclear relationship,” Dean, now a vice president at the Nuclear Threat Initiative nonprofit, said. President Donald Trump expressed support for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, Russia and China when he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, but they didn’t discuss the possibility of site visits during their talks, a US official said. Xi did not leave the door open to discussing a trilateral agreement, pointing to the US and Russian nuclear arsenals being larger than China’s – a point that Chinese officials have routinely used to shield themselves from any discussions that could lead to limiting their nuclear stockpile before they are on par with the US, the official added. Still, the topic of nuclear arms control has long been a focus for Trump, who is expected to meet with Xi twice later this year. By the time the two leaders meet again it is expected that further lower-level discussions on possible nuclear site visits will have taken place, the sources said. Visiting nuclear sites for on-site inspections have historically been used as a vital verification tool by the International Atomic Energy Agency to be sure that nations are abiding by their commitments to using the facilities for peaceful purposes. Experts and former US officials who spoke with CNN were encouraged by the talks but were not confident that they will immediately lead to concrete progress on a breakthrough agreement. “It has to be taken seriously. It could be a great start,” said a former US official who has engaged China in track two discussions related to strategic stability in recent years. Still, skeptics noted that the Chinese may have floated the idea in an effort to create a positive atmosphere or to appear serious on the topic of nuclear arsenals, said former US officials and experts who questioned the authenticity of such an offer. “In advance of a big summit if the Chinese can put good feelers out there they will do that,” said another former US official who focused on nuclear issues. “It makes them seem more magnanimous as the two sides are engaging.” The Chinese may have a “maligned motivation” they said. About a year ago Trump said that the US would resume nuclear testing on an “equal basis” with China and Russia, but there has been no known US nuclear testing since that pronouncement. The administration earlier this year accused China of carrying out a secret nuclear test in 2020 using a technique known as “decoupling” designed to evade detection by firing the explosion in an empty cavern to minimize seismic shaking. The National Nuclear Security Administration’s nonproliferation directorate conducted 16-ton underground non-nuclear explosion last week at the Nevada National Security Site that was the second in a years-long series of experiments designed to mimic the alleged Chinese test, according to an agency spokesperson. The decoupled test explosion offered NNSA and other entities a chance to validate the effectiveness of new methods and equipment for detecting such stealthy tests. “You cannot evade American innovation,” NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams said in a news release announcing the test. The Trump administration is also working on a proposal that would enable assure verification that low-yield nuclear testing is not happening at nuclear sites and could share that with the P5 group later this year, a US official said. It is unclear what kind of technical equipment could be part of that proposal. Gerald Brown, who studies China’s military at the Council on Foreign Relations nonprofit, said he is “not particularly optimistic” but that the reciprocal visit scheme, if enacted, is “a potential glimmer of hope” for reducing nuclear risk between the US and China. Brown, a former State Department intel analyst, said that China’s ongoing nuclear buildup “is deeply linked with political goals, namely its aggressive ambitions regarding Taiwan.” China historically has viewed nuclear talks as “tool to gain political concessions” on Taiwan, he argued, rather than as a genuine policy goal. “You won’t know what’s on the table until you engage in a thoughtful, rigorous way to see if this is something in our interest — and it might be,” said Dean. Dean, whose nonprofit has engaged with Chinese entities in nonofficial diplomatic discussions in recent months, said he sees mutual “interest and acknowledgement that the risks are real.” He pointed at the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which sparked some of the first US-Soviet risk reduction measures like a 24-hour phone hotline, as a historical warning. “We don’t need to wait for a crisis to start reducing nuclear risks,” Dean argued. “And the risks are very real right now.” Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

title: Buttigieg, Gallego and other potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meeting
content: A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the party’s future, in one of the party’s first major gatherings following the election. Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, according to an initial lineup shared first with CNN. The group of speakers also includes Govs. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, plus several additional members of Congress. The “What’s Next” summit is being hosted from November 12-14 by Majority Democrats, an organization that launched last year to help Democrats win in more places. In staging the event less than two weeks after the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the Senate and the House, the group is looking to move quickly to outline the lessons learned from the election that could be instructive going forward, including in the next White House race. “This isn’t a policy conference nor a talk shop on tactics,” Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, said in a statement. “What’s Next is timed for a unique moment after the midterms and before the presidential to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage.” Organizers chose Denver partly because it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. The initial lineup also includes top party strategists such as David Axelrod, former senior adviser to President Barack Obama and a chief political analyst at CNN; Quentin Fulks, former principal deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024; and Morris Katz, adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Majority Democrats is not the only organization holding an event in the immediate aftermath of the midterms in a bid to shape the party’s future. Two days after the election, some of the party’s most prominent strategists and commentators are set to converge in Washington, DC, for Crooked Con, which is hosted by the progressive media company Crooked Media.
