title: Democrats are taking big chunks of GOP voters in key Senate races, polls show
content: President Donald Trump has never had worse poll numbers with his base than he does ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. And a growing volume of polls shows a significant portion of that base is preparing to cross over and vote for Democrats. New York Times-Siena College polls released over the weekend showed between 9% and 16% of Republican likely voters said they favored the Democratic nominee in five key states: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. And these aren’t the only polls to show a sizable crossover effect — especially in the middle of the country. All told, Democratic candidates have led among GOP voters by double digits in four key Senate races, and they lead by an average of at least 9 points in seven of the top 10 races , according to a CNN review of polling in each state. Democratic candidates also seem poised to take an especially large percentage of Republican voters who don’t identify with Trump’s MAGA movement — often around one-quarter of them. This data comes with an important caveat: Polling in the last few presidential elections has underestimated GOP support. And there are some signs that those misses may have been driven by polls reaching the right number of Republicans overall, but not enough of the party’s — and by extension, Trump’s — strongest supporters. If that pattern holds this year, it’s possible that GOP-aligned voters may wind up more supportive of Republican candidates than the polls suggest now. But it is worth noting that polling in the last midterm election, in 2022, did not exhibit this pattern. Perhaps the most striking numbers in the new Times-Siena polls came in Kansas , which has recently emerged as a surprising battleground. The poll showed Democrat Adam Hamilton tied with GOP Sen. Roger Marshall at 45% among likely voters, with the Libertarian candidate at 5%. So how has Hamilton made the race that close in red Kansas, a state that Trump carried by 16 points in 2024? The pastor has peeled off 16% of registered Republicans and 10% of self-identified Republicans. (By contrast, Marshall took just 2-3% of each category of Democrats, according to the survey.) But Hamilton is not the only Democratic candidate pulling double digits among Republican voters. The Times-Siena poll showed Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek taking 12% of registered Republicans and 5% of self-identified Republicans. And the state representative also took double digits among self-identified Republicans in recent polls from Marist College ( 13% ) and Fox News ( 10% ). In Alaska, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola took 13% of registered Republicans and 9% of self-identified Republicans in the Times-Siena poll. And in Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff was taking 10% of self-identified Republicans in the most recent high-quality poll, from Fox News in late June. Other Democrats take slightly less but still significant numbers. The Democratic nominees in North Carolina (Roy Cooper), Ohio (Sherrod Brown) and Texas (James Talarico) have all averaged 9% of the GOP vote in recent high-quality polls, according to a CNN review. Among other Democrats: New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas was averaging 5%, former Maine state Senate President Troy Jackson was averaging 4%, and Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed was averaging 3%. Thus far, the Democratic Party hasn’t matched the larger advantages in national polling. The so-called generic ballot, which asks people to choose between an unnamed Republican and an unnamed Democrat, shows Democrats averaging about 4% of Republican voters in recent high-quality polls. But the numbers do recall some of Democrats’ results in the 2018 midterms, which was a strong year for Democrats overall. Exit polls back then showed Democrats taking double digits’ worth of GOP voters in a number of states — West Virginia (17%), Arizona (12%), Ohio (11%), Pennsylvania (11%) and Wisconsin (10%) — and taking between 5% and 9% in the rest of the key races. (While Democrats took more than 40 House seats from the GOP and benefitted from a favorable environment in the first midterm election under Trump, they did lose two Senate seats because they were defending some very red states.) This year, Fox News polling also breaks out Republicans between MAGA Republicans and non-MAGA Republicans. And four Democratic Senate candidates have taken at least 21% of the non-MAGA Republicans: Cooper in North Carolina ( 21% ), Talarico in Texas ( 22% ), Brown in Ohio ( 25% ) and Turek in Iowa ( 28% ). El-Sayed took 12% of non-MAGA Republicans in Michigan, while Democrats took 12% on the most recent national generic ballot. And given Trump’s apparent base problems, if Democrats do have a historic night on November 3, that could be a group of voters we’ll be talking a lot about in the aftermath.

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico make final written effort to convince judge to maintain White House access
content: Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico said Monday that the White House had offered no new evidence to support its repeated claims that the news outlets’ reporting has endangered national security. The argument, made in a court filing late Monday, is the companies’ final written effort to convince federal Judge Timothy Kelly to indefinitely maintain White House access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after President Donald Trump revoked their credentialed press access last month. “At every turn since, Defendants have sought to justify the President’s ‘ban on the free press’ with a series of shifting rationales, lurching from unarticulated standards of professionalism to nebulous and pretextual concerns about protecting national security,” the filing reads. “But all the while, the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories.’” Kelly will hold a hearing Thursday on the news outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction, which, if granted, would last for a longer period of time while the case plays out. In late September, Trump announced he was barring the three outlets from covering him at the White House, citing their “negative stories.” CNN, MS NOW and Politico quickly sued, and won back temporary access. In his initial ruling , Kelly said the White House must follow five decades of DC court precedent, which bars the White House from revoking journalists’ press access without first giving them notice and a chance to respond. The lawyers in the Monday filing asked that the judge allow them to show the court why “any further access restrictions” the administration might try to impose “violate the Constitution.” The White House has “persisted in unpredictably targeting Plaintiffs,” the lawyers wrote, including by banning both CNN and POLITICO from Air Force One in recent days. “The Oval Office and Air Force One are this administration’s go-to forum for press briefings,” the lawyers added. “The President may not use Air Force One as a flying press briefing room and then claim standardless discretion to exclude news organizations based on the content of their reporting or their perceived editorial viewpoint.” The judge, a Trump appointee, in his earlier ruling resoundingly batted away the Trump administration’s claims that the ban was necessary because the outlets’ reporting could harm national security. The three news outlets — represented by a single legal team — also have been arguing that the White House has discriminated and retaliated against them in violation of their First Amendment protections as the free press. Late last week, the Trump administration doubled down on their arguments to the judge, claiming the outlets weren’t meeting “standards of professionalism and decorum” because they published sensitive national security details. The administration is unlikely to succeed with Kelly, given his prior ruling and the past precedent he must follow. But once the judge rules following Thursday’s hearing, the Trump administration will be able to quickly go to the court of appeals. Seventy-seven media organizations plus several press coalitions have said in court they also oppose the White House’s attempts to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The mainstream press coalition wrote recently they are still concerned other outlets could be blocked from White House coverage in the future. This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Karoline Leavitt joining Fox News as on-air contributor
content: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will join Fox News as an on-air contributor next month, weeks after stepping down from her prior role to spend more time focusing on her family. Fox News said in a statement that Leavitt “will provide political analysis and commentary” across Fox platforms in her new role, which begins November 1. Leavitt added in a statement provided by Fox that she would bring “the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.” Leavitt, who hails from Atkinson, New Hampshire, moved back to the Granite State with her husband and two young children, a source familiar told CNN. The Fox News release also noted her move. The network agreed to build a studio in her home, the source added. She formerly resided in the Naval Observatory in Washington with her family as press secretary. Trump announced on August 12 that Leavitt was leaving the White House, and he has yet to name a replacement . The last press briefing was on September 3, led by Vice President JD Vance. When Leavitt was on maternity leave earlier in the year, Vance and other Cabinet officials hosted briefings on a rotating basis. Trump told reporters at the White House on Thursday, “We have a lot of people who want that job. I would say many of them are right here,” pointing at Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy. When asked who he’s looking for, Trump joked: “Maybe a guy like Peter.” Leavitt said she left her role as press secretary to devote more time to her two young children, something she said was difficult to achieve in a top post at the White House. She remains in the president’s orbit, however, working at the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC. Leavitt recently spoke at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas and helped host the AI-powered America.gov website launch last week in DC. In recent weeks, Leavitt appeared on Fox News host Sean Hannity’s show and podcast. Another former Trump White House press secretary, Kayleigh McEnany, joined Fox News after her tenure at the podium during the preisdent’s first term.

title: ‘Let Troy be Troy’: How Maine Democrats’ hope to beat Sen. Susan Collins is working to quiet doubters
content: As Democrats enter the homestretch of their longtime quest to defeat Maine GOP Sen. Susan Collins, they are placing their hope in a fifth-generation logger from the state’s rural north who speaks with a distinct Allagash accent, displays an apparent penchant for boba tea and has never been this close to the national spotlight before. This was not how it was supposed to go. But more than two months after Democrats picked Troy Jackson to replace Graham Platner following allegations of sexual assault that Platner has denied, his supporters, critics and other observers agree on one thing. “Troy is definitely unusual,” said Douglas Rooks, a longtime Maine writer and historian who worked in the state legislature when Jackson first arrived there in 2002. “He is very different from anybody who’s been elected in a long, long time from Maine and many other places.” Jackson’s quirkiness is set to be tested in a crucial period of the campaign beginning Tuesday night, when he and Collins are set to meet for the first of four debates in 10 days. And this weekend, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) is set to visit Maine for three rallies with Jackson, testing whether the progressive working-class politics they share play as well in a general election as they do in a primary. “[Jackson] is who he is, and I think in this election, people like that,” said Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington. But he also said Jackson would have a “learning curve” on navigating the Senate compared to Collins that could work against him. Jackson has hit a few road bumps recently. A September story from New York magazine aired out concerns he’s being overly managed by out-of-state consultants, a video of him enjoying a boba tea drew widespread ridicule online, and he had to apologize for theorizing about why Jews may not want to call the war in Gaza a genocide. A CBS News/YouGov poll released Friday showed some warning signs for Jackson. Forty-three percent of Democrats said they wished someone else were their nominee, and nearly a fifth of voters who disapproved of Trump said they still supported Collins. The poll found the Senate race tied. Jackson, who lost his primary bid for Maine governor earlier this year before the Senate nomination came open, is still working to galvanize some former Platner loyalists. Scott Niemi, an organizer who met with Platner in August to pitch him on a write-in campaign that Platner ultimately rejected, said he supports Jackson but raised questions about his ability to excite Democrats. “Obviously he doesn’t carry the same energy as Graham, and he definitely doesn’t have the speaking ability that Graham did,” Niemi said. “I think that’s kind of hurt him the most. We went from someone who’s fiery, had a lot of fight in him, to a guy who’s a bit on the calm side, which I can appreciate, but we want someone who can go to Washington and fight for us.” Jackson has insisted he is staying the course. “Nothing has changed,” Jackson said during a call-in program on Maine radio Thursday when asked about the New York magazine story. “This campaign has the same people working on it that it did during the governor’s race. At the end of the day, this campaign is for anyone and everyone who wants to beat Susan Collins and Donald Trump and have a government that works for them.” Cathy Breen, a Jackson supporter who served with him in the state Senate, said he is “in brand new waters, which I’m sure is disorienting.” But she said she was confident in his campaign and strategy, noting he “absolutely knows what happened” in 2020 when Maine Democrats nominated a more traditional politician, state House Speaker Sara Gideon, and had their hopes dashed by Collins. “Mainers can smell Washington like nobody’s business, and they don’t like Washington telling them what they do,” Breen said. “I think Troy’s done a really good job of staying true to his story.” Jackson has made at least 50 public appearances since he replaced Platner in late July, according to his campaign. He has leaned into making the race a referendum on Collins’ support for Supreme Court justices who helped overturn Roe v. Wade, an issue that national Democrats believe is key to peeling off women who have historically broken for Collins. Democrats were at least initially excited that Jackson mixed Platner’s outside image with far more government and political experience. But Republicans are working to use his resume against him. “The fact is, Troy is a 20-year Augusta insider, which poses a problem for him, since Mainers know that’s where so many of their biggest problems come from,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a statement. Collins remains under pressure to answer for a recent ProPublica story detailing an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving her office, a report she’s strenuously disputed. And President Donald Trump continues to be a major vulnerability for her in a state where he is deeply unpopular. Some Jackson supporters say his mission is to strike more of a balance between his Aroostook County folksiness and the gravitas that Mainers have come to expect from their senators, including on policy issues. Rooks said the transition from the small world of state politics – the Maine Legislature is part-time – to a federal race can trip up politicians and cause “a lot of vertigo.” “If I were helping him with debate prep, which I am not, my thing would be, ‘let Troy be Troy,’ and let’s just make sure on substance, he’s sharp,” said Nirav Shah, who also tried to replace Platner but dropped out as Maine Democrats coalesced around Jackson.

title: ‘A five-alarm fire’ confronts President Trump in red-state October blitz
content: The midterm elections were just two days away the last time a sitting president visited Grand Island, the fourth-largest city in the middle of one of the nation’s most reliably Republican states. It was November 5, 2006, and George W. Bush was barnstorming red cities in red states in hopes of staving off what would become the inevitable: a wave wiping away Republican control of the House and Senate for the final two years of his term. Now, President Donald Trump is facing the midterm music. As Trump arrived here Monday night, to a state he won by 20 points two years ago, he is looking for a safe harbor – and to fire up friendly faces – in the latest stop on his red-state October blitz. “Everyone here tonight is part of the greatest political movement in the history of the country,” Trump told cheering supporters. “MAGA, MAGA, MAGA!” The White House itinerary tells the story of how the final chapter of the fall campaign is playing out almost entirely in Trump country. In a weeklong stretch, the president’s travels from Texas to Oklahoma to Alabama to Ohio to Nebraska and back to Texas — all states he carried by double digits — underscore the degree to which Republicans are on defense as he urgently rallies supporters to come to his party’s aid. “Just get out and vote,” Trump told a weekend crowd in Ohio. “If you do that, we’re going to win and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.” With or without vulgarities, Trump has been telegraphing his worry about the midterm campaign for the last year. It’s a rare bout of self-reflection that he faces the same challenges all presidents do, with the fight for control of Congress nearly always delivering a comeuppance to the party in power. “Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don’t do well in the midterms,” Trump lamented Friday night at a stop in Mobile, Alabama. “I don’t know why. Nobody’s explained it.” It’s still an open question whether Trump’s sudden campaign spree, along with significant GOP financial advantages in nearly every battleground state, will help Republicans avoid a similar fate now. Democratic anxieties are also rising about being outspent in TV ads across the map. In 2018, during Trump’s first midterm election, Republicans lost the House but narrowly expanded their grip on the Senate. But with a far bleaker economic picture and a lingering war in Iran, even many Republicans are pessimistic about November. “This is a five-alarm fire,” a GOP member of Congress from a state Trump visited recently told CNN, asking to not be identified to avoid alienating the White House. “We always welcome the president, but I don’t know if he’s aware of the feelings out here.” When Trump arrived at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island, he stepped into the state’s 3rd Congressional District, which he won with 76% of the vote in 2024. It’s the most Republican part of Nebraska, covering 80 of the state’s 93 counties, where cattle ranching and farming is the lifeblood of the economy. The president is not visiting the two other congressional districts in Nebraska, which are highly competitive, particularly the 2nd District to fill the seat of retiring Rep. Don Bacon. The 2nd – which includes Omaha and is sometimes known as the “blue dot” – is one of only three districts in the country Trump lost in 2024 that is represented by a Republican. Leading Democratic and Republican super PACs both removed more than $1 million for the race in the 2nd District Monday as Democrats appear confident in their prospects of flipping the seat. Trump’s rally is intended to offer a boost to Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is facing a challenge from Dan Osborn, a former union leader and independent candidate. It is among the competitive races stirring anxiety among Republicans in their effort to hold their Senate majority, where there is no margin for error as the battleground map expands . “There’s no doubt that high fuel prices put a strain on the budgets for every Nebraska family,” said Ricketts, who was invited to the stage Monday night to appear alongside Trump. “That’s one of the things I hear when I travel the state.” “We must stop him,” Ricketts told the crowd. “Get out and vote!” Osborn is running again two years after losing by fewer than 7 percentage points to GOP Sen. Deb Fischer. This time, he faces no Democratic opposition, with the party intentionally standing down in hopes of defeating Ricketts. “The significant difference now between when I was campaigning in 2024 is the war in Iran and costs that are skyrocketing,” Osborn told CNN. “With every single town hall, that’s usually the first thing that gets brought up is the cost of living. It’s tough.” The president’s August decision to allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported into the United States with lower tariffs was also met with fierce opposition from Nebraska cattle growers. The policy, which Trump said was designed to bring down the cost of beef in the grocery store, has also sparked controversy in Iowa , Kansas and Texas , the rest of the top four beef-producing states. All four have competitive Senate races in states Trump won three times. Whether Trump addresses the matter will be closely watched in the region. “This harvest season, with diesel nearly doubled, export markets drying up, rural hospitals struggling, and senseless tariffs still hitting our pockets, Trump would be better served doing his actual job instead of breaking every promise he made to Nebraskans,” said Jane Kleeb, chairwoman of the Nebraska Democratic Party. In his weekend campaign stops, Trump continued to exhibit a disconnect between how he describes the economy and how many Americans experience it. He made no mention of rising costs but said: “With the hottest country anywhere in the world, it’s the golden age of America.” He is striving to make the November election a contrast with Democrats rather than a referendum on him and the administration’s policies. It follows a familiar pattern with his 2018 campaign travel in the midterm election of his first term: visiting red states filled with admirers, hoping to minimize political harm by firing up his detractors. “If the Democrats win, you will end up in a 1929-style Great Depression,” Trump told a crowd in Ohio on Saturday night. “We will have a disaster on our hands.” Excitement built in Grand Island, a city of 53,000, ahead of his arrival. Trump won Hall County, which includes the city, by 37 points in 2024. Local news accounts recalled the last time Air Force One landed at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in 2006. In that speech, Bush warned Republicans against lapsing into a gloom-and-doom mindset. “I’m sure you’ve heard the same predictions I’ve heard,” Bush said. “The prognosticators have already decided the outcome of this election before the good people of Nebraska have voted.” A decade before Trump rallies began leaving their mark on modern-day politics, Bush spent the spent the final four days of that campaign also barnstorming through Montana, Nevada, Missouri, Iowa, Colorado, Kansas, Florida and Arkansas. Republicans held all three House seats in Nebraska then. But they went on to lose their congressional majorities – 31 seats in the House and six in the Senate – in a midterm election season Bush famously described afterward as “a thumping.” This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Shadow minister says Tories would ‘keep political activism out of classrooms’ – UK politics live
content: Laura Trott , the education secretary, has given a speech at the conference. This morning the events are on the main stage, which is the smaller venue. This afternoon events are in the larger symphony hall. Trott’s speech was largely a long rant about supposed political correctness excesses in schools, with pupils being told that white people are privileged, women can have penises, Britain is racist etc. She said the Tories would “keep political activism out of the classroom”. Trott is now taking part in a panel discussion including the Telegraph journalist and GB News presenter Camilla Tominey . Tominey is no leftie, but even she seemed to think Trott had laid it on a bit too thick. Tominey said that, following the supreme court judgment, she thought children were no longer being told women can have penises. There aren’t many people watching – either in the hall or on YouTube, where there is a live feed. But the Labour press office is tuning in. It has just posted this picture of the event on social media with the heading “People disguised as chairs latest” – a reference to a joke told by Jeremy Clarkson yesterday, when he was sarcastically commenting on how good it was to see so many people in the audience for his Tory conference session. It is widely assumed that, under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, moderate, one-nation Conservatives have been more or less wiped out as a force in the party. But, in her Guardian column based on her time at the conference, Polly Toynbee suggests they might be more resilient than we think. Here is an extract. double quotation mark If nothing improves by next conference, the mirage of Badenoch’s rock-solid support will melt away. But what would replace her? Waiting in the wings there is a model of what a Conservative revival might look like – Prosper UK , launched in January. It tiptoes, praising Badenoch loudly, yet it is running seven events at this conference. That included a small Sunday night rally for electoral reform. It was addressed by former West Midlands mayor Andy Street, now co-chair of Prosper UK with Ruth Davidson It is backed by a formidable array of what was once the One Nation group, now defunct in parliament – or dormant under Badenoch’s rightwards march. No MPs back Prosper UK in public, but the group claims a third of them do secretly, along with 30,000 declared supporters . David Gauke, vice chair, has crept back into the party – he thinks by accident when the membership computer processing his re-application didn’t register he’d been ejected in 2019. In returning, he joined a battalion of remainer luminaries of the centre-right who’d had the whip suspended at the same time, including Kenneth Clarke and Dominic Grieve. Gauke travels the country speaking to Conservative associations and others. Prosper UK is pro-EU, pro-migration for skilled workers and foreign students, pro-net zero and against the pension triple lock – and Gauke says that “Conservatives should be truth tellers on all these”. But though socially liberal, he’s dry as a bone on fiscal discipline, campaigning for low business taxes, a smaller state and enticing back non-doms – all Hayek, no Keynes. “No one speaks for some 7 million people centre or centre-right,” he says. And here is the full column. In her interview with Times Radio this morning, Kemi Badenoch hinted that, if Labour has legislated to make the pensions triple lock less generous by the time of the next election, a future Tory government would not reverse that. In his party conference speech last week, Andy Burnham said he wanted to change the triple lock uprating mechanism from 2030, with the savings used to part fund his plans to set up a National Care Service. The government later said it would legislate for this before the election . The Tories are committed to the pensions triple lock in its current form. But, asked if she would repeal any legislation passed making it less generous, Badenoch replied: double quotation mark I have said that the triple lock is our policy and it remains our policy. I don’t think going after pensioners is the right thing when there are loads of people who can work, who won’t work. When we are going to reverse Labour’s policies, I say we are going to reverse their policies. I have said that we are keeping this policy, but if they take that money and they spend it on something that we can’t get it back from, then it would be difficult for me. What I’m not going to do is lie to your listeners just so I can get votes. I tell the truth and I say the triple lock is our policy and we’re keeping it. But what I’m not going to do is to say something when I don’t know what the situation would be about what Labour has done with that money. We have to be very careful. Laura Trott , the education secretary, has given a speech at the conference. This morning the events are on the main stage, which is the smaller venue. This afternoon events are in the larger symphony hall. Trott’s speech was largely a long rant about supposed political correctness excesses in schools, with pupils being told that white people are privileged, women can have penises, Britain is racist etc. She said the Tories would “keep political activism out of the classroom”. Trott is now taking part in a panel discussion including the Telegraph journalist and GB News presenter Camilla Tominey . Tominey is no leftie, but even she seemed to think Trott had laid it on a bit too thick. Tominey said that, following the supreme court judgment, she thought children were no longer being told women can have penises. There aren’t many people watching – either in the hall or on YouTube, where there is a live feed. But the Labour press office is tuning in. It has just posted this picture of the event on social media with the heading “People disguised as chairs latest” – a reference to a joke told by Jeremy Clarkson yesterday, when he was sarcastically commenting on how good it was to see so many people in the audience for his Tory conference session. Air Marshal Greg Bagwell , former deputy commander of RAF Air Command, told Times Radio he did not think the Tories pledge of £10bn over 10 years would be enough to fund a missile defence system that would protect the UK, its territories and bases. As the Press Association reports, Bagwell said: double quotation mark It really is a question of definition of what capability you’re going to deliver here, and what you can realistically expect in terms of protection. You might be able to protect certain key sites, certain strategic areas. London would be an example, but of course that’s not enough. If you’ve got military bases all around the country, you’ve got power stations, you’ve got critical infrastructure dotted around the country, then you’re really going to have to try and cover the entire area, which is is challenging. Bagwell said a full system could cost more than £80bn. He said that the US was talking about spending between $200bn and $1tr (£150bn to £750bn) for their “Golden Dome”. Bagwell’s analysis matches what General Sir Richard Barrons told MPs in the summer. (See 10.23am .) According to the BBC , Sidharth Kaushal , a senior fellow at the defence thinktank RUSI, said that while £10bn would not fund an Israeli-style “Iron Dome” missile defence system, it would “probably cover” what the UK “actually needs” including horizon radar and more E7 aircrafts. According to the Conservatives , a Tory government would fund the plan for a £1bn-a-year “Britannia Shield” with some of the money from the extra £10bn a year it would raise for defence. Last month, the Tories published details of how that £10bn a year would be funded. Some £8bn of that would come from cuts to benefits – £4bn from cutting housing benefit, £3bn from reimposing the two-child benefit cap, and £1bn from the Motability scheme funding cars for disabled people. The housing benefit cuts would partly be achieved by cutting local housing allowance (LHA) rates, which determine how much people can receive in housing benefit. The Tories have briefed that LHA rates would be set at 10th percentile of local market rates, not the 30th percentile. The cuts would also involve social sector rents being cut. Kemi Badenoch was asked earlier (see 7.59am ) about General Sir Richard Barrons , the retired former head of Joint Forces Command, saying an Iron Dome-style missile defence system would cost up to £100bn. Barrons gave these figures to the Commons defence committee in evidence in July on the defence investment plan (Dip) . This is what he said when asked about what was missing from the Dip. double quotation mark The subject of integrated air and missile defence also links to the absolutely vital point that gets lost so often: the defence investment plan is the articulation of the SDR [strategic defence review] – it is the things that made the cut for the money available. Given the legacy holes in defence, there is at least another half of the iceberg that never made it into the DIP, because it was not even remotely affordable. There is a £60 billion to £80 billion hole in defence infrastructure—falling down airfields, ports, housing, the Reserve Forces’ and Cadets’ Associations. Most of that is not in the DIP, because it just could not get into the cut. Integrated air and missile defence is the iconic thing that did not make into the review. There is about £1 billion in the DIP for it, and that buys improved command and control – you’ll know better that you’re going to be hit by a missile – some improvements for the Air Force ability to shoot down cruise missiles, and some improvements to the Type 45 so that it has a better capability against ballistic missiles. Many people in the country assume there is a sort of iron dome over at least London, and that is not even remotely there. Even if you embrace the extraordinary technological change that some companies are producing in low-cost kills, whether directed energy weapons, DragonFire or cheaper missiles like Cambridge Aerospace and that kind of thing, the cost of an iron dome at entry level is probably £80 billion over 10 years—entry level. The IAMD [integrated air and missile defence] of my dreams is probably £120 billion over 10 years. But we got £1 billion, because it sits in that bit of the iceberg that never got to be remotely affordable. We should not kid ourselves that if we have an argument about the margins of the DIP, we are somehow fixing defence. That is just not true. Here is Jessica Elgot ’s story about the Tory “Iron Dome” spin gaffe. As Jess points out, the Conservatives did not just call their plan an Iron Dome in their press release; Kemi Badenoch used the phrase too, in an article published under her name in the Sun. Kemi Badenoch is now on GB News. Talking about the Tory plans for a “Britannia Shield”, she says: double quotation mark It is not an Iron Dome like what Israel has. It is not something used to cover the entire country. This is her final interview from the morning round, and it ends with Badenoch, even more firmly then before, quashing the line that the Conservatives were using in a news release (see 7.59am ) sent out less than 24 hours ago. In her interview on Times Radio earlier, Kemi Badenoch said she had been reading about how some “heritage brands” recovered after losing their reputation for tips that might help the Tories. She said: double quotation mark I’ve been reading a lot about heritage brands that lost their way. And it always happens when the brand stops looking after its core customers and starts doing things that are off-brand. And it takes some time to recover from that. But that is what I’m doing. Refreshing the brand. I’m glad that I’m doing well. I know that people have started listening to the Conservative party again. I want them to start buying. Q: What do you think of the US pulling out of RAF Fairford? Badenoch says this is very serious. The UK needs to take defence more seriously. Q: How worried are you about the party’s polling? Badenoch says she wants people to know the party is under new management. Q: Are you ready for an election? Badenoch says there is a difference between being ready for an election and ready for government. She is ready for both, she claims. Kemi Badenoch is now on LBC. Nick Ferrari is asking how many missile defence units there would be. Badenoch says she cannot give Ferrari the technical details. She says he should speak to James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary. Q: But did you not ask how many units would be needed? Badenoch says she focused on outcomes. She says Cartlidge, a former defence procurement minister, is across the detail. Q: Why should people trust the Tories with something like this when they could not deliver HS2? Badenoch says her booklet, The Right Way, addresses what went wrong with government procurement under the Tories. Balls asks Badenoch about Suella Braverman telling ITV last week that she never considers herself of English ethnicity . Q: How do you feel about that? Badenoch says she does not understand why people are policing others’ identity. double quotation mark I don’t understand why all of a sudden some people are policing other people’s identity? I think identity is something very personal. If that’s how [Braverman] feels about herself, I think that’s fine. But what I’m worried about is politicians running around telling some people that they’re not English. I remember when I was younger watching English footballers, black and white. I can’t imagine people pointing to the black footballers and saying, ‘Well, you’re not really, really English.’ I think we need we need to be very careful with this, sort of conversation. She says, on gender, she thinks men are men and women are different. But identity is different. Her children are half white, half black. Q: But isn’t Braverman saying that black footballers playing for England are not English? Badenoch says Braverman must speak for herself. She says she personally would not say those footballers are not English. Q: Do you think Kemi Badenoch would be welcome as a migrant to the UK today? Badenoch says when she was born in England in 1980 thinks were very different. Two years later the rules were changed. (Badenoch gave British citizenship because she was born in the country, but that rule changed.” Ed Balls and Susanna Reid are presenting. Q: Will you cut inheritance tax? You have called it immoral. Badenoch says she has called it too high. But she won’t announce cuts until she has found the money to fund them. She was very moved by what farmers told her about the impact of inheritance tax, she says. Q: So you might cut it, rather than abolish it. Or raise the threshold at which it is paid. The government is expected to raise £15bn from it by 2030. Badenoch says she does not accept all those figures. She says the country is getting poorer. She says she was surprised Andy Burnham did not talk about the economy in his speech.

title: No queues, empty seats and the worst speech ever heard: welcome to the Tory conference
content: A t the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham floated the idea of electoral reform. This week in Birmingham, the Tories have come up with a plan of their own: voting with their feet. How to put this nicely? Let’s just say that the Conservative party conference is extremely civilised. No queues for the food concessions. No queues to get into any of the halls. In fact, the organisers are delighted that anyone has turned up at all. This doesn’t feel like a high-octane meeting of a party preparing for government. More like a home counties meeting of the Rotary Club. On current evidence, if there is a general election next year – as Kemi Badenoch is trying to convince us there will be – then the Tories won’t be active participants. More like vaguely disinterested observers. For these four days, Birmingham is a city where you can sit and watch the world pass you by. Not that those who have turned up seem unhappy. Rather, they are thrilled to find themselves still alive. This time last year, there was a possibility that they faced extinction: under threat from left and right and with a leader in Kemi who looked unlikely to last six months. Since then things have stabilised as Robert Jenrick has been stopped from pulling out their ventilator in the intensive care unit. They are now merely an endangered species. The conference centre is a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of the Tory party in a protected habitat. The morning’s activities take place in what is optimistically called the main hall: a hard-to-find side room with a capacity of about 200. These are way more seats than any of the acts require. First up was shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, who managed to bore even himself. Still, at least the hall was about a third full. Which, for Rich, is a major result. I’m guessing most of the people there were family and friends. It was no fuller for the shadow health secretary, Damian Hinds, who stumbled over his notes for five minutes. Weirdly, there were 24 people watching an empty stage online after he had left, while only 17 had been online when he was talking. Or maybe that’s not so weird. For the afternoon offering we were moved to a slightly bigger hall. This could have been a mistake. It had come billed as a “major speech by the shadow chancellor”. Only we were made to sit through an hour and a half of nothingness – an opportunity to deliberate our own and the Tories’ existential futility – before the main event. By now at least another third of the audience had left. A wise choice. They clearly had some idea of what was coming. Even 20 minutes of Andrew Griffith can rip your soul in half. If only I had joined them. Not that the hall was anywhere near full to begin with. First up was the shadow Defra secretary, Victoria Atkins , who had sensibly worked out that no one in their right mind would stay to hear her talk. So instead she positioned herself as a cable TV presenter – there were 53 people watching online – chatting to her guest, Jeremy Clarkson. This did at least lift the mood in the hall. A genuine celeb was among them for 15 minutes. However, it doesn’t say much for your conference when your most popular speaker is someone who openly says he’s not a Tory party member and has only turned up because he will go anywhere people will have him to talk about farming. “Wow,” said Jezza. “There’s an awful lot of people here dressed as seats!” Vicky giggled nervously. The rest of the chat came and went perfectly amiably. Jezza did what he does best, giving his best impression of a multimillionaire held back by the incompetence of government. Still, at least he injected some fun. Vicky wanted to know how the farming summer had gone. He replied that the Diddly Squat farm had produced several ounces of hen food because of the extreme heat. Someone should have told him that Griffith was about to get rid of the Climate Change Committee. If you missed any of this, you will be able to watch extended highlights on the next series of Clarkson’s Farm. From then on, the conference became one long car crash. A panel with a couple of rightwing hacks droning on about nothing and then another panel in which one businesswoman congratulated herself on not getting stabbed on the train to Brum – apparently all her friends refuse to use trains – and then a businessman sobbing at the thought of billionaires being asked to pay inheritance tax. Some of them are so sick with worry they can no longer sleep. Finally the main attraction. What would turn out to be a landmark occasion for all party conferences. Because Griffith proceeded to give the worst speech ever heard. Not just in content but in delivery. It was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey. Constantly applauding himself and ending his sentences with “Yeah”. What was left of the audience didn’t know where to look. If Andy really is the future chancellor, then we are truly fucked. Even Mel Stride wasn’t this hopeless. We might as well all pack up now. He was going to build more homes that were uninsulated and might fall down because they were cheaper. He would cut taxes and regulations the Tories had themselves introduced. “This is our destiny,” he said. And then he dematerialised. It was as though he had been primitive AI and his controller had seen quite enough and decommissioned him. Andy didn’t know he had finished. And neither did anyone else.
